analysis.one_liner: Removes FCC rules that bar one company from owning a daily newspaper and broadcast stations in the same market.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; it was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Communications Commission to wipe out its newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership rule within 90 days, letting any company own a daily newspaper and radio or TV stations at the same time, including through commonly controlled affiliates. The rule was designed to keep multiple local news voices in one community from being controlled by a single owner. The bill was introduced with three cosponsors, sent to committee and a subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Media companies that publish a daily newspaper and want to buy AM, FM, or TV stations in the same market, or vice versa, plus large consolidated owners whose combined newspaper-broadcast holdings would gain value once the ownership cap disappeared.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Newspaper publishers and broadcast station owners

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the FCC to modify its rule 47 C.F.R. 73.3555 by eliminating any provisions limiting the grant or renewal of an AM, FM, or TV broadcast license based on the owner's ownership or control of a daily newspaper [S3].
It requires the FCC to finish those rule changes within 90 days of enactment, so the deregulation could not be stalled by the agency [S3].
The CRS summary describes the same mandate: the FCC must modify its regulations to remove limits on granting or renewing broadcast licenses to parties owning or controlling a daily newspaper [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Local news audiences. Fewer independent owners in a market means fewer competing editorial voices covering local news, and the rule's elimination removes the main federal safeguard against one company controlling both a town's leading newspaper and its broadcast stations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Local news audiences and competing media voices

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith case for the bill was that in an era of internet competition, the decades-old cross-ownership rule treated newspapers as if they faced no rivals; owners argued they needed combined newspaper-broadcast operations to keep local outlets financially viable [S3].

The cost an honest supporter would acknowledge: lifting the rule lets one company in a market control a newspaper and broadcast stations simultaneously, which reduces the number of independent editorial voices and the diversity of local news coverage the rule was written to protect [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is written narrowly and cleanly: it targets one FCC rule and gives the agency 90 days to act [S3]. But its substance is a one-way deregulation for media owners. Any efficiency argument rests on a market-competition rationale; the tangible public effect is fewer independent local news voices, with no offsetting public benefit in the bill. For a working reader, the trade is industry convenience for reduced local news diversity.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House, referred to the Commerce Committee, then sent to its Telecommunications subcommittee, and never advanced to a hearing, markup, or floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Oxley introduced the bill on February 4, 1999 with cosponsors Rep. Cliff Stearns and Rep. Ralph Hall of Texas [S3].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce [S5].
On February 24, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill sat in subcommittee until the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the FCC's newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership rule stayed in force, and media companies kept the ban on owning a market's newspaper and broadcast stations together. Local news audiences kept the rule's diversity protection; broadcasters and newspaper publishers lost the chance to consolidate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Local news diversity, since the FCC rule survived

for.name: Rep. Michael G. Oxley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to direct the FCC to eliminate the newspaper-broadcast cross-ownership restrictions.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 4, 1999 and sent it to the Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection Subcommittee; the committee never brought the bill to a markup or the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only three cosponsors, two Republicans and one Democrat, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape of support is too thin to call.

industries.industry: Broadcast television and radio station owners
industries.note: The bill would have freed broadcasters from the rule barring them from also owning a daily newspaper in the same market, expanding their acquisition options. The cost falls on the public's local news diversity, since it removes the safeguard against one company controlling a community's newspaper and broadcast outlets.
Newspaper chains could have bought or operated AM, FM, and TV licenses in their own markets. Their gain comes at the expense of independent competing voices in local news coverage.

industries.industry: Local independent media and competing news voices
industries.note: Cross-ownership limits exist partly to preserve independent local outlets; eliminating the rule would put smaller independent media at a disadvantage against combined newspaper-broadcast operators. The bill died, so this loss did not occur.
